old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the oft and leg stump.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. 16

old_digest: When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “NoBall.”
new_digest: When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “No Ball.”
When a wide is called the ball does not become “dead” and the batsman may be out stumped or run out.
An over should always be finished, unless a wicket fall within two minutes of time (see Law 45), or unless there is a local rule extending the time.

A Batsman cannot be stumped off a No Ball (Law 16). The Laws of Cricket clearly make a distinction between the wicket-keeper and the fieldsmen and between cases of “stumping” and “run out” (see Laws 23 and 28). When a No Ball has been called it must be left to the Umpire to decide, on the facts before him, whether the case is one of “stumping” (under Law 23) or “run out” (under Law 28).

old_digest: A Batsman may be out lbw, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.
new_digest: A Batsman may be out l b w, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.

old_digest: Was it part of the batsman’s person which intercepted the ball? It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an lbw with a breaking ball.
new_digest: Was it part of the batsman’s person, other than the hand, which intercepted the ball? It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an l b w with a breaking ball.

old_digest: If in running, or at any other time, when the ball is in play he be out of his ground, and his wicket be struck down by the ball after touching any fieldsman, or by the hand or arm, with ball in hand, of any fieldsman;—“Run out.” It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets—the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the ball had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.
new_digest: If in running, or at any other time, when the ball is in play he be out of bis ground, and his wicket be struck down by the hall after touching any fieldsman, or by the hand or arm, with ball in hand, of any fieldsman—“Run out.” It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets —the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the nail had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.

old_digest: (See Notes on Law’ 22.) Although that run which is being attempted shall not be scored it is not the custom for the remaining batsman to resume his position at the wicket he has left if he and his partner have crossed. 12
new_digest: (See Notes on Law 22.) Although that run which is being attempted shall not be scored it is not the custom for the remaining batsman to resume his position at the wicket he has left if he and his partner have crossed. When a run has been made off a no-ball the no-ball should be scored although the ball has been caught. 12

old_digest: He may have passed the howling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off the bails. A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws.
new_digest: A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws, he may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off the bails.

old_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side. 13
new_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side.

The intention of this Law is that the injured striker’s ground, when he has a substitute to run for him, is at the wicket keeper’s end. He himself can only be run out at that end as provided for in the latter part of the Law.

The effect of this Law is that the Umpire shall decide whether the delay of the individual amounts to a refusal of the batting side to play. It provides a specific penalty in such a case but none for the individual.
